title: Lower bounds on fluctuations beyond the distribution classes P(d) and P+(d)
statement: Extend the results of the paper beyond the distribution classes P(d) and P+(d); in particular, prove the fluctuation lower bounds under minimal assumptions on the distribution of the underlying randomness.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on lower bounds for fluctuations of Euclidean combinatorial optimisation and first-passage percolation after 2017. Found the later Bates-Chatterjee and Damron-Hanson-Houdre-Xu work on two-dimensional first-passage percolation and moderate-deviation papers, but nothing that removes the distributional hypotheses of the source's method in general. Kept open.

attempt.method: Read off what the distribution classes are doing in the method. The engine is the source's Lemma 1.2: for X and Y on a common space, P(a <= X <= b) <= (1/2)(1 + P(|X-Y| <= b-a) + d_TV(L_X, L_Y)). One needs a coupled perturbation Y that is cheap in total variation but moves X by the conjectured fluctuation scale.
attempt.result: The role of P(d) and P+(d) is to make a TILT of the underlying product measure both admissible and computable: for i.i.d. coordinates tilted by a parameter delta, the total variation cost of n coordinates is of order delta sqrt(n) and the induced shift of a Lipschitz functional is of order delta n times its mean sensitivity. Setting delta = c n^{-1/2} makes the cost O(1), which is exactly the requirement of Lemma 1.2, and produces a fluctuation lower bound of the order of the resulting shift. So the hypotheses are not about the functional at all; they are about the existence of an exponential-family tilt with a computable Hellinger cost. The minimal-assumption version of the problem is therefore: for which laws mu on the coordinates does there exist a one-parameter family mu_delta with H^2(mu, mu_delta) = O(delta^2) and a monotone effect on the functional? For any mu with a nondegenerate absolutely continuous part this is available; the genuinely hard case is a lattice mu with atoms, where a tilt cannot move the support.
attempt.obstruction: For discrete weights the only available perturbations are resamplings, which change the total variation by an amount bounded below by the atom sizes, so one cannot make the cost o(1) while moving the functional. That is the same wall as item (6) of the same list (discrete edge weights in first-passage percolation), so the general problem and the discrete problem are one obstruction, not two.
attempt.key_identity: An exponential tilt of n i.i.d. coordinates by delta has total variation cost of order delta sqrt(n) and shifts an additive functional by order delta n; delta = n^{-1/2} makes the cost O(1) and the shift sqrt(n), which is the method's calibration.

title: Convergence of the variance of the stochastic travelling salesman tour length
statement: In the travelling salesman problem for n uniformly distributed points in [0,1]^2, prove that the variance of the length of the optimal tour converges to a constant as n tends to infinity, and identify this constant if possible. Chatterjee attributes the conjecture to Mike Steele.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the variance of the Euclidean TSP tour length and its convergence. The standing results are the Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley law of large numbers, the Rhee-Talagrand concentration bounds, and the source's own lower bound of order 1; no proof of convergence of the variance was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what structure would make a variance converge, and check whether the TSP functional has it. Convergence of Var to a constant is what a functional with a local (stabilizing) representation does, via an add-one-cost martingale decomposition.
attempt.result: The natural route is stabilisation: if the tour length admits a representation as a sum over points of a local add-one cost that depends only on a neighbourhood of radius O_P(1) after rescaling to intensity one, then the Penrose-Yukich central limit theorem gives both a CLT and convergence of the normalised variance to a constant expressed as an integral of a two-point add-one correlation over the Poisson process. The identification of Steele's constant is then automatic in the same formula. So the conjecture is a stabilisation statement, and its difficulty is exactly that the TSP tour is a GLOBAL constraint: inserting a point can reroute the tour arbitrarily far away. The known partial substitutes - Rhee-Talagrand concentration - bound the variance from above by a constant but do not establish stabilisation, and an upper bound of constant order plus the source's lower bound of constant order still leaves the limit unproven.
attempt.obstruction: The TSP is not known to stabilise. The best available locality statement is that the optimal tour is close to optimal on cells of a partition (the boundary-functional method of Redmond and Yukich), which controls the mean to O(sqrt(n)) but leaves an error in the variance of the same order as the variance itself. Making the boundary error o(1) requires an estimate on the number of tour edges crossing a fixed line, which is what nobody can control.
attempt.key_identity: For a stabilising functional the variance converges to an explicit Poisson add-one-cost integral, and Steele's constant would be that integral; the whole conjecture is that the TSP tour stabilises.

title: Tight fluctuation lower bound for Euclidean minimal matching
statement: Prove a tight lower bound for the fluctuations of the length of the minimal matching when the points are uniformly distributed in [0,1]^d.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on fluctuations of the Euclidean minimal matching. The optimal-transport literature (Ambrosio-Stra-Trevisan and successors) gives sharp asymptotics for the MEAN of the matching cost in d = 2 and its logarithmic correction; fluctuation lower bounds of matching order were not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the dimension dependence to decide what 'tight' should mean, since the answer is not the same in all d. For n uniform points in [0,1]^d the minimal matching cost has mean of order n^{1-1/d} for d >= 3 and n^{1/2} (log n)^{1/2} in d = 2.
attempt.result: In d >= 3 the matching cost is a sum of n contributions each of order n^{-1/d}, and the local structure is genuinely local (the optimal matching is stabilising in the sense that a point is matched within distance O(n^{-1/d}) with a stretched-exponential tail), which is why a central limit theorem is expected and the fluctuation order should be n^{1/2 - 1/d}. In d = 2 the matching is NOT local - the Ambrosio-Stra-Trevisan analysis shows the cost is governed by the Gaussian free field at all scales, and the fluctuation order should then be read off from the field, not from a sum of local terms. So 'tight lower bound' means two different theorems in the two regimes, and the source's list does not separate them. That separation is the useful output: the source's coupling method should be calibrated against a local tilt in d >= 3 and against a global (field-level) tilt in d = 2.
attempt.obstruction: In d = 2 the field-level heuristic predicts fluctuations of order (log n)^{1/2} for the total cost, which is smaller than the mean by a factor n^{1/2}, so any tilt used in Lemma 1.2 must move the cost by only (log n)^{1/2} while costing O(1) in total variation - an extremely fine calibration, and one that the crude n^{-1/2} tilt of the source's Bernoulli example cannot supply.
attempt.key_identity: Minimal matching of n uniform points has mean cost of order n^{1-1/d} for d >= 3 but n^{1/2}(log n)^{1/2} in d = 2, and the d = 2 cost is governed by a log-correlated field, so the fluctuation problem splits into a local and a field-level case.

title: Fluctuation lower bound for the longest common subsequence of random words with uniform letters
statement: Prove a tight lower bound for fluctuations in the longest common subsequence problem for random words. Chatterjee notes that considerable progress has been made but that the most important case of UNIFORMLY distributed letters is open, and that a solution would complete the proof of the central limit theorem for longest common subsequences, as shown by Houdre and Islak.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on variance lower bounds for the longest common subsequence of random words. The Houdre-Islak central limit theorem (conditional on a variance lower bound) and the Houdre-Ma results on central moments are the standing references, together with the non-uniform-letter results the source cites. No proof for uniform letters was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask why uniformity is the hard case rather than the easy one, since it is the most symmetric.
attempt.result: Because the method needs an asymmetry to tilt. For non-uniform letter distributions one perturbs the letter frequencies: raising the probability of the most common letter increases the expected LCS at a computable rate, and the total variation cost of the tilt is controlled - exactly the calibration of item (1). Under the uniform distribution the first-order effect of any frequency tilt VANISHES by symmetry (the derivative of the LCS mean with respect to a symmetric perturbation of the simplex is zero at the symmetric point), so the leading term of the shift is second order in delta while the cost stays first order, and the calibration delta = n^{-1/2} that made the method work now gives a shift of order n^{1/2} times delta = O(1) rather than the required sqrt(n). This identifies the exact reason uniform letters resist the method, which the source records only as 'the most important case is open'.
attempt.obstruction: To recover a first-order effect at the symmetric point one must tilt in a direction that is not a frequency change - for instance, a correlation between the two words - but any such tilt breaks the independence of the two sequences, and then the total variation cost is no longer a product-measure computation. This is the same difficulty as constructing a non-product perturbation in item (1).
attempt.key_identity: At the uniform letter distribution the derivative of the mean LCS with respect to a frequency tilt vanishes by symmetry, so a tilt of total variation cost O(1) moves the LCS by O(1) rather than by sqrt(n); the method's calibration fails at first order precisely at the symmetric point.

title: Improving the fluctuation lower bound for two-dimensional first-passage percolation
statement: Improve the lower bound for the fluctuations of the first-passage time in two-dimensional first-passage percolation.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on first-passage percolation variance lower bounds. Newman-Piza and Zhang give a variance lower bound of order log n; the search returned that 'Bates-Chatterjee and Damron-Hanson-Houdre-Xu give a lower bound of sqrt(log N) for the fluctuations of the passage time in two dimensions', which is the fluctuation-order statement of the source's own method. The conjectured order is n^{1/3}, so the gap remains enormous. Kept open; I did not read the Bates-Chatterjee paper, only its description.

attempt.method: Compare the achieved order with the calibration of Lemma 1.2 to see what an improvement would require.
attempt.result: The sqrt(log n) bound is exactly what a tilt supported on the whole box gives: the passage time to distance n depends on order n^2 edges, a uniform tilt of size delta costs delta n in total variation, so delta = 1/n, and the shift produced by such a tilt is delta times the number of edges ON the geodesic, i.e. delta times n, which is O(1) - the sqrt(log n) comes from summing scales dyadically. To reach n^{1/3} one must tilt only the edges near the geodesic, of which there are order n, giving a cost delta sqrt(n) and a shift delta n, hence a shift of sqrt(n) at unit cost - too big, so the true constraint is that the tilt must be chosen adapted to the geodesic and the adaptivity destroys the product structure. This says the barrier is not the size of the tilt but its MEASURABILITY: an efficient tilt must know where the geodesic is, and then L_Y is no longer a product measure and d_TV is not computable.
attempt.obstruction: Any geodesic-adapted perturbation is a function of the very randomness being perturbed, so the two laws in Lemma 1.2 are not related by a fixed change of measure. Circumventing this needs a two-step argument in which the geodesic is localised first, which is precisely the transversal-fluctuation problem (exponent xi), itself open in d = 2.
attempt.key_identity: A uniform tilt over the n^2 edges of the box has cost delta n and moves the passage time by delta n, giving only O(1) at unit cost; an efficient tilt must charge the O(n) edges on the geodesic, and locating them is the transversal fluctuation problem.

title: Fluctuation lower bounds in first-passage percolation with discrete edge weights
statement: Extend the lower bound result for first-passage percolation to the case of discrete edge weights.
status_search: Same search as E0033. The Newman-Piza log n variance lower bound covers {0,1}-valued weights; a fluctuation-order (concentration-function) lower bound for discrete weights by the source's method was not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Identify the exact failure of the coupling for atoms, and look for a substitute perturbation that is available in the discrete case.
attempt.result: With continuous weights the perturbation is a small shift of each weight, whose total variation cost is proportional to the shift; with weights on a lattice the smallest available move is a resampling, whose cost is bounded below by a constant times the number of resampled edges divided by nothing - i.e. resampling m edges costs an amount of order m p, where p is the smallest atom, and this cannot be made o(1) unless m is bounded. The substitute that remains available is a RANDOM-CLUSTER style perturbation: change the weight of each edge independently with probability eps and, on the changed edges, resample. Then d_TV is at most eps times the number of edges, and the shift of the passage time is at most eps times the geodesic length. The ratio shift/cost is then the same as in the continuous case, so the method's calibration is NOT lost by discreteness; what is lost is the monotone control of the shift, since a resampled edge can lower as well as raise the passage time and the effects cancel to first order. The honest conclusion is that discreteness costs the SIGN, not the size, of the perturbation.
attempt.obstruction: Recovering the sign needs a positive-probability event on which the resampling raises the passage time by a definite amount, which in turn needs a lower bound on the number of pivotal edges of the geodesic - and the number of pivotals is exactly the quantity whose fluctuation one is trying to bound. Newman-Piza avoid this by working with the variance rather than the concentration function, which is why their result exists for {0,1} weights and the fluctuation-order statement does not.
attempt.key_identity: Resampling each edge independently with probability eps has total variation cost of order eps times the number of edges and shifts the passage time by at most eps times the geodesic length, so the shift-to-cost ratio survives discreteness; what fails is that the shift has random sign.

title: Any nontrivial fluctuation lower bound for first-passage percolation in dimension at least three
statement: Prove any nontrivial lower bound for the fluctuations of the first-passage time in higher dimensions. Chatterjee notes that a lower bound of order 1 is easy using the method of the paper.
status_search: Same search as E0033. Recent work on 'properties of first-passage percolation above the hypothetical critical dimension' surfaced but was not read; it concerns the conjectured d >= d_c regime rather than a fluctuation lower bound in d = 3. Kept open with that lead recorded.

attempt.method: Ask why the two-dimensional dyadic-scale argument does not simply repeat in d = 3.
attempt.result: The two-dimensional sqrt(log n) comes from summing an O(1) contribution over the log n dyadic scales, and each scale contributes because a box of side 2^k contains a bottleneck that the geodesic must cross and whose weight can be tilted. In d >= 3 the geodesic can go AROUND a perturbed region at a cost that is second order in the perturbation, because the box has many more disjoint crossings: the number of edge-disjoint paths across a box of side L in d dimensions is of order L^{d-1}, so the effect of tilting a fixed fraction of one crossing is diluted by L^{d-2}. That dilution factor, which is 1 in d = 2 and grows in d >= 3, is precisely why the same argument gives only O(1) in higher dimensions. Naming the dilution exponent d-2 is the useful step, and it predicts that the method as it stands cannot produce more than a constant in any d >= 3 without a new idea, rather than merely being unproved there.
attempt.obstruction: To beat the dilution one needs to perturb a whole cutset rather than a path, and a cutset in d dimensions has L^{d-1} edges, so the total variation cost of tilting it grows like delta L^{(d-1)/2}, while the induced shift is only delta times the local weight change on the crossing actually used. The ratio degrades with d, and no substitute perturbation with a better ratio is known.
attempt.key_identity: A box of side L in Z^d carries of order L^{d-1} edge-disjoint crossings, so tilting one crossing is diluted by L^{d-2}; the exponent d-2 is exactly the gap between the two-dimensional argument and higher dimensions.

title: Improving the lower bound on the Newman-Piza exponent in two dimensions
statement: Improve the lower bound for the Newman-Piza exponent chi' for two-dimensional first-passage percolation.
status_search: Same search as E0033. Newman-Piza show that the log n variance lower bound can be improved to a power of n in directions where the limit shape is not flat, and that under a finite radius of curvature assumption power-law lower bounds and an inequality between chi and xi follow. No unconditional improvement was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Separate the conditional from the unconditional statement, since Newman-Piza's power bound is conditional on curvature of the limit shape.
attempt.result: The whole difficulty is that the two available routes need opposite inputs. The curvature route gives chi' > 0 but assumes a strictly convex limit shape - a statement about the shape that nobody can prove for any nondegenerate weight distribution in d = 2. The coupling route (the source's) is unconditional but gives only sqrt(log n). A third possibility, and the one worth stating, is that curvature is not needed in full: the Newman-Piza argument uses curvature only to guarantee that geodesics to nearby endpoints are asymptotically disjoint, and that disjointness is a weaker statement than curvature. Reformulating the required input as 'geodesics to two endpoints at angular separation theta are disjoint outside a ball of radius o(n)' is a strictly weaker hypothesis than strict convexity and is the natural target. This is a reformulation of the hypothesis, not a removal of it.
attempt.obstruction: Even the weaker disjointness statement is unproven: the only unconditional information about the limit shape in d = 2 is that it is convex, compact, and has the lattice symmetries, and it is not known to be strictly convex anywhere, or differentiable anywhere except at the boundary of the percolation cone.
attempt.key_identity: Newman-Piza's power-law lower bound uses curvature of the limit shape only through asymptotic disjointness of geodesics to angularly separated endpoints, which is strictly weaker than strict convexity.

title: Positivity of the Newman-Piza exponent in higher dimensions
statement: Show that the Newman-Piza exponent chi' is strictly positive in higher dimensions.
status_search: Same search as E0033 and E0036. Kept open.

attempt.method: Combine the dilution computation of E0035 with the curvature route of E0036 and see which one degrades faster in d.
attempt.result: They degrade in opposite ways, which is the point worth recording. The curvature route needs less as d grows in one respect - the limit shape in high d is expected to be closer to a ball, hence more plausibly strictly convex - but the geodesic-disjointness input needs more, because two geodesics in d dimensions have more room to run alongside each other without meeting, so angular separation no longer forces disjointness in any quantitative way. The coupling route degrades monotonically in d by the dilution factor L^{d-2}. So neither route improves with dimension, and the natural conjecture chi' > 0 in all d has no method behind it at all - which distinguishes item (9) from item (8), where at least a conditional theorem exists.
attempt.obstruction: There is no dimension in which both the shape input and the disjointness input are available. Above the conjectured critical dimension the fluctuations are expected to be Gaussian with chi = 0, so a proof of chi' > 0 valid in ALL d >= 3 would be false if that prediction is right - the problem as stated is therefore implicitly restricted to d below the (unknown) critical dimension, and identifying that dimension is itself open.
attempt.key_identity: The coupling route's dilution L^{d-2} grows with d and the curvature route's disjointness input weakens with d, so no known method improves with dimension; and above the conjectured critical dimension chi is expected to vanish, so the statement cannot hold for all d.

title: Optimality of the fluctuation lower bound for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick free energy and ground state
statement: Improve the lower bound on the order of fluctuations of the free energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, or show that it is optimal. The same for the ground state energy.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 covered by the fetch of the 2025 survey 'Free energy fluctuations in SK and related spin glass models: a literature survey' (source sk_free_energy_survey_2025 in this intake), which records the state of the art: Gaussian fluctuations of order 1/N in the high-temperature phase (Aizenman-Lebowitz-Ruelle), Chen-Lam at the critical temperature, and the low-temperature regime open. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what the conjectured order is in each phase, since 'optimal' means different things above and below the critical temperature, and check which phase the coupling method can see.
attempt.result: Above criticality the free energy has Gaussian fluctuations of order 1/N (in the normalisation where the free energy is O(1) per spin), and the coupling method's tilt - perturbing the disorder matrix by an independent Gaussian of size delta - costs delta N in total variation and shifts the free energy by delta times the overlap-weighted energy, so the calibration reproduces the right order. Below criticality the conjectured order is N^{-5/6} times a Tracy-Widom-type law for the ground state, and the source's method cannot see it because the shift of the free energy under a tilt is governed by the Gibbs average of the perturbation, which in the replica-symmetry-breaking phase is not concentrated. So the honest statement is that the method is calibrated in the phase where the answer is already known and blind in the phase where the question is open.
attempt.obstruction: In the low-temperature phase the response of the free energy to a disorder perturbation is a Gibbs average over a non-concentrated overlap distribution, so the shift in Lemma 1.2 is itself random of the same order as the fluctuation being bounded. Breaking that circularity requires control of the overlap distribution at the level of its fluctuations, which is what the Parisi formula does not give.
attempt.key_identity: A Gaussian tilt of the SK disorder of size delta costs delta N in total variation and shifts the free energy by delta times a Gibbs-averaged energy; in the replica-symmetry-breaking phase that average is not concentrated, so the shift is as random as the quantity being bounded.

title: Optimality of the fluctuation lower bound in the random assignment problem
statement: Prove the optimality of the lower bound in the random assignment problem for cost distributions in P+(1) or any other general class of cost distributions.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on fluctuations of the random assignment problem after Aldous's zeta(2) limit and Wastlund's exact formulas. The mean is known exactly (Wastlund, Linusson-Wastlund, Nair-Prabhakar-Sharma), but the order of fluctuations is not; no optimality proof was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the exactly solvable structure, which this problem has and the others on the list do not. For exponential costs the expected optimal assignment cost on K_{n,n} is exactly the sum over k <= n of 1/k^2, and Wastlund's method computes it by a recursive exact identity.
attempt.result: The exact formula fixes the mean but not the variance, and the reason is structural: Wastlund's recursion computes an EXPECTATION by an exchangeability argument that does not lift to second moments, because the increments it telescopes are not independent. The conjectured fluctuation order is n^{-1} (so that the cost is zeta(2) + Theta(1/n)), which coincides with the order of the largest single term of the exact sum - and that coincidence is the natural target: prove that the fluctuation is dominated by the last few terms of the telescoping. This gives a concrete route that the source's list does not name, and it is a route, not a proof.
attempt.obstruction: The telescoping increments are strongly negatively correlated (adding a row makes the next row's marginal gain smaller), so the variance of the sum is much smaller than the sum of the variances and cannot be estimated term by term. The source's coupling method needs a tilt that moves the cost by n^{-1} at unit total variation cost, and a tilt of n^2 exponential costs by delta costs delta n and moves the assignment cost by delta, giving delta = 1/n and a shift of 1/n - so the calibration is exactly critical here, which explains why the source obtains the right order but not optimality.
attempt.key_identity: Tilting n^2 i.i.d. exponential costs by delta costs of order delta n in total variation and shifts the optimal assignment cost by order delta, so the shift-to-cost calibration is exactly critical at the conjectured fluctuation scale 1/n.

title: Fluctuation lower bounds for linear eigenvalue statistics and extreme eigenvalues of patterned random matrices
statement: Prove tight lower bounds for fluctuations of functionals of random matrices other than the determinant, such as linear statistics of eigenvalues and the maximum and minimum eigenvalues, in ensembles where such results are not known. This includes patterned random matrix ensembles such as random Toeplitz and Hankel matrices and random band matrices.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on fluctuations of linear eigenvalue statistics for Toeplitz, Hankel and band matrices. Central limit theorems for linear statistics exist for Toeplitz and Hankel ensembles (Chatterjee, Liu-Sun-Wang and successors), which give fluctuation lower bounds where they apply; the extreme eigenvalues of these ensembles remain far less understood. Kept open, with the CLT literature recorded as covering part of the linear-statistics half.

attempt.method: Split the request into its two halves, because they have opposite difficulty profiles: linear statistics are smooth functionals of the whole spectrum, extreme eigenvalues are non-smooth functionals of its edge.
attempt.result: For linear statistics the coupling method is well calibrated: a Gaussian tilt of the n independent entries of a Toeplitz matrix (there are only order n of them, not n^2) costs delta sqrt(n) and shifts a linear statistic by order delta n times the derivative of the test function, so delta = n^{-1/2} gives a shift of sqrt(n) - and since linear statistics of patterned ensembles have fluctuations of order 1 (no n^{1/2} normalisation), the method is far from tight and the correct calibration must exploit cancellation. For extreme eigenvalues the shift under a rank-one-like tilt is bounded by the tilt's operator norm, which for a Toeplitz perturbation of size delta is delta times sqrt(n log n), so the method predicts fluctuations of at least n^{-1/2} times that, i.e. of order sqrt(log n) - almost certainly not tight. Recording that the two halves need different calibrations, and that the linear-statistics half is the one where the method overshoots, is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: Patterned ensembles have order n independent entries but n^2 matrix entries, so the entries are heavily dependent and the total variation cost of a tilt is computed on the wrong space; the shift, in contrast, lives on the matrix. Reconciling the two requires the Jacobian of the map from symbol to spectrum, which for Toeplitz matrices is singular at the edge - precisely where the extreme-eigenvalue question lives.
attempt.key_identity: A random Toeplitz matrix has only order n independent entries, so a tilt costs delta sqrt(n) rather than delta n; the shift it induces on the spectrum is governed by the symbol-to-spectrum Jacobian, which is singular at the spectral edge.

title: A distributional limit theorem in any of the examples of the paper
statement: Prove a distributional limit theorem in any of the examples discussed in the paper: the stochastic travelling salesman problem, the stochastic minimal matching problem, the random assignment problem, the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, first-passage percolation, or random matrices.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 covering the same examples. Distributional limits exist in the high-temperature SK phase (Aizenman-Lebowitz-Ruelle) and for some patterned-matrix linear statistics, so this item is partly addressed for two of the six examples; for the Euclidean optimisation problems, the random assignment problem and first-passage percolation no distributional limit is known. Kept admitted, with the two partially-covered examples recorded.

attempt.method: Ask what a distributional limit needs beyond a matching pair of bounds, and identify which example is closest.
attempt.result: A limit law needs an approximate decomposition of the functional into asymptotically independent pieces. Of the six examples, the one with such a decomposition in sight is minimal matching in d >= 3, where the optimal matching is expected to stabilise and the Penrose-Yukich machinery would give a Gaussian limit outright; the source's own list separates matching (item 3) from the limit-theorem request (item 13) but the two are the same theorem in that dimension range. In first-passage percolation the expected limit is not Gaussian but Tracy-Widom, so no decomposition into independent pieces can exist and the request is of a completely different nature there. Pointing out that item (13) is really two requests - a Gaussian one for the stabilising examples and an integrable one for first-passage percolation - is the useful separation.
attempt.obstruction: For the stabilising candidates the missing ingredient is stabilisation itself (see E0030 and E0031). For first-passage percolation a Tracy-Widom limit is currently only reachable through exact solvability, which nearest-neighbour first-passage percolation does not have; every known Tracy-Widom result in the KPZ class uses a determinantal or Yang-Baxter structure absent here.
attempt.key_identity: The six examples split into stabilising ones, where a Gaussian limit would follow from an add-one-cost decomposition, and first-passage percolation, where the expected limit is Tracy-Widom and no decomposition into asymptotically independent pieces can exist.
